reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Bailey & Love (paediatric surgery)
clinicalPearls: The most common congenital chest wall deformity, characterised by an inward depression of the sternum and adjacent costal cartilages producing a sunken appearance
It is often noticed in early childhood and typically becomes more pronounced during the adolescent growth spurt
Many patients are asymptomatic, and the main concern is cosmetic and psychological, particularly body-image distress in adolescents
Severe depression can displace and compress the heart and reduce exercise tolerance, causing exertional breathlessness or palpitations in some patients
There is a recognised association with connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and with scoliosis, which should be looked for
Severity is commonly quantified with the Haller index derived from CT, comparing chest width with the narrowest sternovertebral distance
Surgical correction, when indicated, is most often by the minimally invasive Nuss procedure using a retrosternal bar, or by the open Ravitch technique
Non-operative options such as vacuum bell therapy may benefit selected younger patients with milder, flexible deformities
reference.pathophysiology: Pectus excavatum results from abnormal, excessive growth of the costal cartilages that pushes the sternum posteriorly, creating a concave anterior chest wall. The precise cause is unknown but is thought to involve disordered cartilage growth, and there is a familial tendency and links with connective tissue disease. In marked deformity the depressed sternum can compress and rotate the heart and reduce the space available for cardiac filling, which may impair cardiopulmonary performance, particularly during exertion.
additionalDifferentials: Poland syndrome (with chest wall and pectoral muscle hypoplasia)
Marfan or other connective tissue syndrome with chest involvement
Acquired chest wall deformity after thoracic surgery
additionalInvestigations: CT or MRI of the chest to calculate the Haller (or correction) index and assess cardiac compression
Echocardiography to evaluate cardiac displacement and function
Pulmonary function testing to assess any restrictive impairment
Cardiopulmonary exercise testing in symptomatic patients
Assessment for connective tissue disorders and scoliosis where suspected
redFlags: Progressive exertional dyspnoea or exercise intolerance suggesting significant cardiopulmonary compromise
Echocardiographic evidence of marked cardiac compression or displacement
Features of an underlying connective tissue disorder such as Marfan syndrome
Arrhythmia or syncope on exertion warranting cardiac evaluation
reference.prognosis: The deformity itself is rarely dangerous, and many patients do well without surgery. Operative correction in appropriately selected patients generally produces good cosmetic and functional results with high satisfaction, though the retrosternal bar requires later removal and there is a small risk of recurrence.
pitfalls: Dismissing the condition as purely cosmetic and overlooking genuine cardiopulmonary symptoms
Failing to screen for associated connective tissue disorders and scoliosis
Offering surgery based on appearance alone without objective severity and functional assessment
Underestimating the psychological impact on adolescents
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Observe mild, asymptomatic deformity, as many patients do well without intervention
Offer non-surgical vacuum bell therapy and exercise or physiotherapy programmes for flexible or milder chest-wall depression
Correct severe or symptomatic deformity surgically, using the minimally invasive Nuss bar procedure or an open Ravitch repair, with later planned bar removal
Address body-image distress with psychological support, particularly in adolescents
Screen for and manage associated conditions, notably Marfan syndrome and scoliosis
Assess cardiopulmonary impact with imaging, echocardiography and exercise testing to guide the decision to operate, and refer symptomatic patients to paediatric or thoracic surgery
